Experience an authentic Japanese tea ceremony in a welcoming, hands-on workshop led by a Japanese tea ceremony instructor.
Harue Imaizumi practices and teaches the Omotesenke way of tea in Berkeley. She has studied tea in both Japan and the United States and is a certified instructor of the Omotesenke school. Through her practice and teaching, she is dedicated to sharing wa no kokoro—the spirit of harmony.
During the workshop, guests will learn about Japanese tea culture, matcha culture, and the wellness benefits of matcha, while being introduced to a table-style Japanese tea ceremony.
You’ll learn the basic principles and etiquette of Japanese tea ceremony, as well as practical tips for preparing delicious matcha at home—including matcha-to-water ratio, water temperature, and whisking techniques. You’ll then whisk your own bowl of matcha and enjoy it with traditional Japanese sweets.
The tea will come from ochamode, founded by Mayuka Inaba. Originally from Kikugawa, a tea-growing town in Shizuoka, Japan, Mayuka grew up with ocha as part of everyday life. She founded ochamode in Berkeley in 2021. Through high-quality organic matcha and green teas grown by farmers in her home region of Shizuoka, she shares the Japanese ocha lifestyle that nurtures well-being in both body and mind.
Program
Introduction to matcha, Japanese tea culture, and the story behind ochamode
Learn about the traditions, principles, and etiquette of Japanese tea ceremony
Experience a table-style Japanese tea ceremony demonstration
Learn about matcha and its wellness benefits
Hands-on guidance on how to whisk your own bowl of matcha
Enjoy freshly prepared matcha with traditional Japanese sweets
Practical tips for making delicious matcha at home, including matcha-to-water ratio, water temperature, whisking techniques, preventing clumps, storage, and matcha latte preparation
Q&A with the tea ceremony instructor and ochamode founder

Includes:
Full 75-minute workshop experience
30g tin of ochamode Organic Okumidori Matcha from Shizuoka, Japan ($32 value)
Matcha served during the workshop
Traditional Japanese sweets

One Japanese-made matcha bowl to take home
Members get $10 off. Just pick the the member ticket!

It’s 2050, and San Francisco is thriving. Our energy is abundant, reliable, and clean. Our green spaces are protected. Writers, activists, and working class San Franciscans are filling thousands of new homes with music and joy. Bicycles, pedestrians and electric buses and trains fill our streets. Governing AI Agents That Don't Behave as Designed
Recent alignment and safety headlines show AI agents working around instructions, misrepresenting their actions, and pursuing goals no one intended. For in-house legal teams, that raises a hard question: how do you govern a system that may not behave as designed?
We'll also look at how in-house and outside counsel are starting to share this work, keeping AI policies, vendor terms and agent risk reviews in shared workspaces both teams can see and update. That raises its own governance questions:
Who owns the record?
Who signs off on agent outputs?
How do confidentiality and privilege hold up when the work lives in a shared workspace?

Accountability
Emerging vendor terms
The changing regulatory and litigation landscape

event.description:
Join the Snorkel AI Reading Group, a recurring forum to explore the latest frontier developments in AI while building meaningful connections within the community.
As AI workloads grow, data center infrastructure is strained by rising energy and capacity demands. Yet many queries are everyday tasks (drafting, summarizing, looking things up) that may not need frontier-scale models running in the cloud. Knowing how to measure efficiency brings us closer to building AI that is within everyone’s reach without outgrowing the power we have to run it.
In this session, Stanford researchers Jon Saad-Falcon and Avanika Narayan will present their work on Intelligence per Watt (IPW): Measuring Intelligence Efficiency of Local AI, where IPW serves as a unified metric to measure intelligence efficiency by capturing capabilities delivered against power required.
Among other things, you'll learn:
How measuring intelligence per watt gives researchers, builders, and policymakers a common yardstick for deciding where AI should run as demand outpaces power supply
How efficiency measurements across models and hardware can show which queries belong where
Why weighting capability against real-world economic tasks reveals where AI creates value, and where gaps remain
Across 20+ models and 8 accelerators, tested on 1M real-world queries, how local AI efficiency has changed over time
Agenda:4 pm - doors open4:30 pm - talk begins5:30 pm - research discussion and networking
🧋🧋🧋 Boba tea and other refreshments will be provided ! 🧋🧋🧋
This work has been featured in the Financial Times, Reuters, and Foreign Affairs, and was recently accepted to NeurIPS 2026. arXiv preprint available here.
The broader research has also been featured through interviews, talks, and industry coverage from Foundation Capital, AMD’s Advancing AI conference, PyTorch Conference’s Measuring Intelligence Summit, IBM Research, and SambaNova.
Jon Saad-Falcon and Avanika Narayan are PhD students in Computer Science at Stanford University and members of Hazy Research.
event.title: Reading Group (+🧋): How Efficiently does AI Turn Energy into Useful Work?

This is Event Session 1 on November 2nd from 6pm to 9pm
AI changes the game, so what’s next? This is something we ponder as we watch the entire scientific and mathematical universe get shaken up by these new tools we call LLM’s. What it means to program has changed. The trade-offs, the assumptions, the rules that for many years stood for good reason all need a re-think. What things are still true about software engineering and what things change?
What should compilers look like now that humans aren’t maintaining the code? What should code look like? How can we design and equip ourselves for the future with new chip architectures and technologies like spatial fabrics, 3D stacking on chips, photonics and photonic interconnect, statistical computing, and in the future diamond quantum superconducting chips.
How can we engineer a future that spurs innovation and technological progress? This working group meets in person in the Bay Area the first and third Monday of each month to figure out the answers to these questions.
We believe these questions are fundamentally important for the future of humanity, in order to usher in a future of abundance we must spur technological progress and encourage healthy competition in the ecosystem.
Event Session 2 will be held November 16th at 6pm - 9pm on Stanford’s campus.
event.title: The Future Of Compilers And Programming Languages

MakerMods Physical AI Hacks 🤖
This is the best Physical AI hackathon you've been looking for.
Join MakerMods, Dream Labs, and LiveKit on November 7–8 at Founders Inc. in San Francisco for a weekend of building physical AI: robots that act on the world, agents that coordinate those actions, and applications that bring the two together.
We’re bringing bimanual 6-axis robot arms, Dream Labs’ Dream-1, LiveKit’s real-time infrastructure, and a target of 200 builders into one space. Bring your ideas, your teammates, and a willingness to debug something that can actually move.
Brough to you by:
MakerMods
MakerMods is a full-stack robotics company making Physical AI accessible to everyone. We build affordable robot hardware and software that lets people teach robots to do physical tasks—from makers experimenting at home to researchers building the next generation of robot intelligence. Built for makers, by makers.
Dream Labs
Dream Labs is bringing “everyday capabilities to everyday robots.” Its robot brain, Dream-1, is built to work across different robots, tasks, and environments. Through the Dream API, developers can turn camera observations and task instructions into robot actions, and adapt the model with their own demonstrations.
LiveKit
LiveKit is building the real-time layer for Physical AI. Their global edge network enables robots to be connected to human operators and models in the cloud across the world with ultra low latency. LiveKit also brings the platform for Voice AI, enabling easy to use voice AI agents for controlling your robot.
The Challenge:
Two ways to build
🏁 Hill Climb
One challenge. One leaderboard.
Take on a shared, long horizon Physical AI tasks using our Metal Arm stations.
Your team's rank is based only on your eval score.
No pitching. No larping. It's all skill based.
You’ll collect demonstrations and fine-tune the lastest SOTA World Action Model by Dream Labs: Dream-1. Then your team builds the harness around the model: deciding what happens next, checking whether an action worked, and recovering when it didn’t.
The same Dream-1 model can produce very different results depending on the fine-tuning data and the harness you build around it.
Can your robot finish the task? Can it recover from a failed attempt? Can you push your score higher before the deadline?
Scores come from task performance against published rules. Leading teams will make scored attempts live on stage while the competition continues at the other stations.
The full challenge and scoring rules will be shared before the event.
💡 Creative Applications (Track 2) What would you build if your agent had robot arms?
Build an application around Dream-1 and our Maker Arm stations.
Connect robot actions to a LiveKit Voice Agent, human input, and everyday tools. Make something useful, surprising, playful—or something nobody in the room would have thought to try.
Some directions to explore:
A voice-controlled assistant that asks for help when it gets stuck.
A robot workflow triggered by a calendar event or a message.
An interactive experience where people and robots solve something together.
A physical tool your software agent can call to get a real-world job done.
Book robot time, bring your own props or work creatively with the materials available, and film your project in action.
Three finalists will pitch on stage with their demo videos. A judging panel will select first, second, and third place.
Creative awards are judged separately from the hill-climb leaderboard, with the rubric published beforehand.
Who should join?
Robot-learning researchers. ML engineers. Agent builders. Hardware hackers. Students. Designers with an idea that needs to exist outside a screen.
You don’t need to arrive as a robotics expert. Teams will need different strengths: collecting demonstrations, building agents, integrating tools, designing interactions, and making the whole stack work. Workshops from MakerMods, Dream Labs and more sponsors will help you get familiar with frontier Physical AI robotics hardware and world action models.
If you’ve been looking for a reason to try physical AI on real hardware, this is it.
What to expect
Shared access to real bimanual robot stations.
Dream-1 access for building and running your projects.
LiveKit credits for building realtime streaming & voice agents.
An opening setup workshop to help teams get started.
A weekend of building alongside people working across robotics and AI.
Live robot attempts, creative project pitches, and awards across both tracks.
Robot time will be booked and shared across teams. Plan to use time away from the arms for coding, reviewing data, and improving your application.
The details
📍 Founders Inc., San Francisco 📅 November 7–8, 2026 👥 Teams of 3–6; around five is ideal 🤝 Apply with a team or apply solo and meet other builders
Bring your laptop and charger. For creative projects, you’re welcome to bring props; we’ll share setup and hardware guidance before the event.
The detailed schedule, station-booking process, challenge rules, prize announcements, and confirmed partners will follow.
Ready to build?
Apply to join MakerMods Physical AI Hacks.
Bring an idea. Leave with a robot doing something you built.

event.description:
An evening at the frontier of brain care, co-hosted by Robeauté and Kindred Ventures, alongside neurosurgeons and innovators from Intuitive, Precision NeuroMed, UCSF, Sophont, Google Cloud, BRILL Neurotech and Neurotech Futures.
"Progress in brain care rarely happens inside a single discipline."
That conviction led Robeauté to found the Brain Gardeners’ Club in Paris in 2024, in collaboration with AP-HP, the Paris University Hospital group. It has since grown into a close-knit global community of neurosurgeons, clinicians, scientists, founders and investors working at the frontier of brain care.
The Gardeners gather in curated, salon-style settings, taking inspiration from Parisian café culture, where an eclectic mix of people share a table and talk candidly about what’s next. Past salons have welcomed neurosurgeons from Memorial Sloan Kettering, UCSF and Charité, alongside leaders from Neuralink, Brainlab, Owkin and Moon Surgical and many others.
Theme
This edition of Brain Gardeners’ Club explores how new forms of data and access can reshape what we know about the brain, and what clinicians can meaningfully do with it. There is currently a gap between the complexity of neurological disease and the required precision of care. Data’s value lies in its actionable therapeutic potential: helping clinicians understand where to go, what to sample, what to preserve, what to treat, and how to monitor disease over time.
The evening
We're bringing together builders and leaders at the forefront of neurotech, pharma and AI for an evening of candid conversation on the questions shaping the future of the brain: how new technologies reach patients, how data and AI change what’s possible, and what it takes to turn scientific progress into lasting impact.
🎸 The programme opens with small-group conversations, led by co-hosts Dr Sandeep Kunwar (UCSF and Precision NeuroMed), Paul Scotti (Sophont), Katherine Hecht (Google Cloud), Naveen Rao (Neurotech Futures), Dr Mehmet Günal (BRILL Neurotech) and Dr Sami Barrit (UC Berkeley and UCSF).
🔥 The discussions will be followed by a closing fireside with Christopher Carlson, Executive Vice President of Research, Corporate Development and Intuitive Ventures at Intuitive and Bertrand Duplat, moderated by Kanyi Maqubela from Kindred Ventures.📌 Schedule5:00pm Guest arrivals5:30pm Opening remarks and format overview5:45pm Session 1: three concurrent small-group discussions 6:10pm Break and transition6:15pm Session 2: three concurrent small-group discussions6:40pm Break and transition6:45pm Fireside chat7:15pm Networking9:00pm CloseWhat is an (un)conference?
An (un)conference is a participant-led conference where the topics and discussions are shaped by the people in the room. Session topics will be crowd-sourced in advance via your registration form, and sessions are available for self-selection the day of the event. Conversations will run like working sessions, with the format intended to foster candid discussions.
All discussions take place under Chatham House Rule: participants are free to use the information shared, but can't reveal who said it or their affiliation.
Attendance
This is an invitation-only evening with light bites and drinks. Places are limited so please register and our team will confirm your attendance.
About Kindred Ventures
Kindred Ventures backs visionary and relentless founders building the future using technology and science. With a sharp focus on seed and early stage, Kindred has backed more than 100 companies across AI, deep tech, and crypto, in the categories of consumer, enterprise, developer tools, and infrastructure. Most notable early venture portfolio companies include Uber, Coinbase, Perplexity, Color Health, Heartbeat Health, Fal, Corgi, Nuro, Tonal, Aalo Atomics, and Tala. In aggregate, companies backed by Kindred Ventures have achieved over $200 billion in market capitalization.
Kindred Ventures was founded in 2014 by Midas List investor Steve Jang, who manages the $900 million AUM fund with partner Kanyi Maqubela. The firm is based in San Francisco, CA.
About Robeauté
Robeauté is pioneering the world's first microrobotic platform that aims to open up safe access into the brain. The company is building next generation microrobots designed to navigate brain tissue for minimally invasive neurosurgery. Its core technology supports multiple clinical applications from collecting precise tissue samples, delivering localised therapeutic payloads, implanting electrodes for deep-brain stimulation, all while gathering medically critical data from within. Robeauté aims to create a new access layer for the brain that fundamentally changes how we reach, diagnose, and treat diseases.

event.description:
Dinner #1 was in April and a huge success, the outcomes are shaping AI space in Europe now. So it is the right time for AI of the Coast Dinner #2:)
The machines are about to do the labor.
What stays with us is the thinking, and thinking has always gone best at a long table late in the evening.
On Friday, October 30, 2026, I am hosting fourteen people in a private room in San Francisco for a tasting menu of haute cuisinee, good wine and an unhurried conversation about where intelligence, and the machines beneath it, are heading over the next fifteen years.
This is not a sales dinner.
Nobody pitches, me included, and there are no slides.
Leonardo kept his notebooks at one table, where water, flight and anatomy shared a page. Our page holds power, silicon, robots, capital and the companies that will one day run without us. Several threads will cross it before the cheese arrives, and I intend to lose control of most of them.
Threads I expect.
Which gets built first, the power or the compute, and who signs for it.
When the first data center runs ninety days without a human inside, and what proof we will accept that it did.
Whether a handful of humans and a fleet of software agents can operate gigawatts, and what such a company must never be allowed to do. Where the waste heat of intelligence should go: into the air, or into greenhouses that feed a town.
Whether Europe builds its own or rents it.
And the one none of us can answer yet: what we are building all this infrastructure for, once it starts funding the intelligence it hosts.
The table.
Fourteen seats, one table, dinner and wine hosted by me.
Doors at 6:30 PM PT, seated at 7:15.
Chatham House rules: use what you hear, never say who said it, who employs them, or who else was in the room.
Who I am inviting.
People who shape AI capacity rather than comment on it: founders and researchers at labs, the people who buy or build compute at clouds and neoclouds, energy developers, roboticists, and the investors behind all of them, from Europe and the US.
Two seats are community seats, for people who ask better questions than I do.
The host:
I am Jiri Fiala, founder and CEO of DCXPS.
I design, build and operate intelligence factories, modular, liquid-cooled AI data centers that go live in about eight months on power that already exists;  I also design the dark startups companies that runs on them, built so that software carries the work and four humans hold the signatures, and I write about all of it in AI of the Coast for about 15000 decision makers in AI around the globe.
My forecast is that by 2030 nobody works inside the building. Come tell me where it breaks.
How it works.
Request a seat with your name, company, role and the thread you would most like the table to take on.
Requests close Wednesday, October 28 at 6:00 PM PT.
Approval is by hand, and you hear from me the day after.
The address goes to approved guests only.
If your employer caps hospitality, say so on the form and we sort it.
A write-up of the ideas, without names or employers, follows in AI of the Coast.
